newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO demands details of Bosnian training centre.
newsitem.headline: NATO demands details of Bosnian training centre.

text.p: The Bosnian federation army has been forced to delay the construction of a U.S.-funded military training centre because the NATO-led peace force has demanded to review details of the project, NATO officers said on Tuesday.

U.S. General William Crouch, the commander of the alliance-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR), has refused to approve construction of the centre until the federation provides a more detailed account of its plans, officers said.
"SFOR has asked for additional details," said an officer who asked not to be named.

The training centre, located near the western town of Livno near the Croatian border, is part of a $400 million U.S. military aid programme devised to strengthen Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation army.
SFOR's response reflected misgivings among some officers in the peacekeeping mission that the American "train and equip" programme could increase the likelihood of another war in Bosnia.

SFOR officers said they expected the training centre to win approval eventually but they insisted that the federation fully disclose its construction and training plans to avoid raising tensions with the rival Bosnian Serb military.
"If everybody knows what's going on up front, things usually go well here," said another officer. "But we're not going to allow something to be slipped through the back door."
The federation wants to construct firing ranges for tanks and artillery at the training centre and to conduct battle exercises for federation battalions, U.S. advisers said.
SFOR, assigned the task of enforcing a peace treaty, wanted to check if the training exercises planned at the site would exceed limits set by a Balkan arms control agreement.

Under terms of the arms control pact, if training exercises employ more than 1,500 troops, 25 tanks, 40 artillery pieces or 40 armoured combat vehicles, rival armies have the right to send observers or to lodge a protest to international monitors.
U.S. advisers in the "train-and-equip" programme chose the rural site around Livno last year because it allows for training and firing exercises to be held a safe distance from any town.
The "stabilisation" programme is supposed to bring a military balance to the region by bolstering federation forces which were outgunned during the 1992-95 conflict.
The opening of the training centre, initially scheduled for the spring, has already been delayed by a dispute among Moslem and Croat federation partners over funding.
The dispute was settled earlier this month, with the Croats agreeing to contribute about $2 million to the $17.5 million project, Western officials said.
